description: Oyuncuların kendi uzay görevlerini tasarlayıp yönetebileceği eğitici ve etkileşimli bir oyun geliştirmeyi hedefliyoruz. Oyuncular; bütçe, enerji ve kütle gibi sınırlı kaynaklarla uzay aracı ve bilimsel ekipman seçerek kararlarının görev başarısını nasıl etkilediğini keşfedecek. NASA’nın açık kaynaklarından yararlanarak bilimsel temeli olan, anlaşılır ve eğlenceli bir deneyim oluşturmak istiyoruz.
summary:
**PROJECT ARES-NEXUS: EARTH TO MARS** is an interactive, browser-based, 2.5D isometric aerospace engineering and Mars exploration simulation developed by Lagrange Works for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

The project takes players on a complete journey from Earth to Mars, combining spacecraft engineering, mission preparation, launch operations, interplanetary travel, planetary landing, and the establishment of a sustainable Martian outpost.

Unlike traditional space games, ARES-NEXUS connects engineering decisions across every stage of the mission. Spacecraft configuration, payload selection, energy production, life-support systems, scientific exploration, and emergency management influence one another, creating meaningful consequences for mission success.

Through interactive environments, astronaut operations, real-time telemetry, scientific challenges, and interconnected resource systems, players experience the complexity of human space exploration while learning fundamental aerospace engineering principles.

Built with HTML5 Canvas, JavaScript, and CSS, ARES-NEXUS combines educational simulations with engaging gameplay, encouraging systems thinking, scientific curiosity, and practical problem-solving.

**Our vision is to make the engineering challenges of humanity's journey to Mars accessible, understandable, and exciting for the next generation of explorers and engineers.**
details:
PROJECT ARES-NEXUS: EARTH TO MARS

Developed by Lagrange Works | NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

1. Project Overview and Purpose

PROJECT ARES-NEXUS: EARTH TO MARS is an interactive, browser-based, 2.5D isometric space exploration and engineering simulation developed by Lagrange Works.

Our project explores a fundamental question in human space exploration: What does it actually take to design, launch, land, operate, and sustain a human mission on Mars?

Rather than treating a Mars mission as a collection of disconnected tasks, ARES-NEXUS brings spacecraft engineering, orbital operations, astronaut safety, resource management, scientific exploration, and settlement sustainability into one interconnected experience.

Players begin by preparing their mission on Earth. Their engineering decisions influence launch performance, the spacecraft's journey, the equipment delivered to Mars, and ultimately the survival and operational capabilities of the surface outpost.

The central objective is to establish a sustainable scientific presence on Mars through informed decisions, engineering problem-solving, and effective mission management.

Our goal is to make complex aerospace engineering principles accessible, interactive, and engaging without presenting simplified game mechanics as certified engineering calculations.

2. Earth Mission Preparation and Spacecraft Engineering

The experience begins at an interactive Earth-based space complex featuring four operational areas:

Vehicle Assembly Building (VAB): Players configure spacecraft and mission hardware, evaluate component specifications, manage payload capacity, and investigate engineering constraints.

Mission Control Center: Players review flight dynamics, mission readiness, trajectory considerations, communication systems, and operational requirements.

Science and Payload Laboratory: Scientific instruments, mission equipment, experiments, and supplies are prepared and evaluated against available spacecraft capacity.

Launch Control Center: Final launch preparations, ground-system checks, and launch operations take place.

These locations are represented as navigable environments with interactive consoles and connected engineering systems.

The mission preparation system incorporates multiple deterministic checks to evaluate spacecraft configuration and operational readiness. Its GO/NO-GO process identifies potential problems and directs the player toward the relevant facility or workstation.

Engineering decisions consider factors such as spacecraft mass, thrust-to-weight ratio, approximate delta-v, propulsion capability, available power, payload limitations, and operational margins.

A particularly important feature is the relationship between Earth-based engineering and Mars surface operations. A payload that exceeds the landing system's allowable mass must be revised, while removing important supplies may create resource limitations after landing.

This creates a meaningful engineering trade-off: solving one problem can introduce another.

3. Launch, Interplanetary Transfer, and Mars Landing

Once mission requirements are satisfied, the spacecraft proceeds through the launch preparation and flight sequence.

The simulation connects vehicle rollout, launch countdown, ascent, staging, Earth parking orbit, Trans-Mars Injection, interplanetary transfer, Mars approach, and Entry, Descent, and Landing (EDL).

Flight information and mission telemetry help players understand the consequences of their earlier spacecraft configuration decisions.

The transfer experience represents the relationship between Earth, Mars, and the spacecraft through an accelerated visual simulation. Mission time and gameplay time are distinguished to communicate the immense duration and distances involved in interplanetary travel without requiring players to wait for real-world months.

The flight and landing models are educational approximations inspired by established aerospace engineering principles, including orbital mechanics, propulsion performance, and atmospheric entry constraints.

Rather than presenting the journey as an instantaneous transition, ARES-NEXUS connects mission planning and spacecraft operation to the eventual conditions encountered on the Martian surface.

4. Mars Surface Exploration and Astronaut Operations

Following arrival, the gameplay shifts to a Martian environment presented through an interactive 2.5D isometric world.

The surface experience focuses on connected operational regions, terrain navigation, scientific exploration, infrastructure deployment, and the safe operation of a human expedition.

The mission includes four astronauts with complementary operational responsibilities. Players can directly interact with crew members, navigate the environment, and coordinate mission activities.

Astronaut operations incorporate movement, task assignment, equipment requirements, and safety considerations. The aim is to combine the immediacy of direct character control with the strategic depth of managing multiple simultaneous mission objectives.

Rovers provide additional mobility and support the movement of equipment and supplies across the Martian terrain.

Cargo handling and construction are connected to actual mission resources. Building an operational outpost requires more than selecting a structure from a menu: equipment availability, material requirements, transportation, and infrastructure readiness matter.

Habitat systems and astronaut activities introduce practical challenges associated with living and working in an environment fundamentally different from Earth.

5. Resource Management and Life-Support Engineering

One of the most important elements of ARES-NEXUS is its interconnected resource simulation.

The mission models the relationships between:

  • Electrical power generation, storage, and consumption
  • Oxygen availability and life-support demand
  • Water storage, consumption, and recovery
  • Food supplies and crew requirements
  • Habitat infrastructure and operational capacity
  • Scientific equipment and communication resources

These systems are intentionally interdependent.

For example, oxygen production may consume both water and electricity. Water recovery requires energy, while scientific equipment and habitat systems compete for the same available power.

Changes in electrical generation therefore influence more than a single numerical indicator. They can affect life-support reliability, equipment operation, and the expedition's ability to continue its scientific objectives.

The simulation differentiates resource quantities, production rates, consumption rates, and operational reserves where appropriate.

Players must balance immediate survival requirements with longer-term investments in scientific productivity, infrastructure, and sustainability.

The objective is not simply to accumulate resources, but to develop an operational system capable of responding to changing environmental and engineering conditions.

6. Scientific Exploration, Research, and Mission Objectives

Scientific exploration is integrated into the broader mission rather than presented as an unrelated collection of achievements.

Players participate in evidence-based activities involving scientific observations, exploration tasks, instrument operation, and research objectives.

The project connects scientific progress to engineering capabilities and mission requirements.

Research activities are designed around meaningful evidence and validation, encouraging players to understand why a scientific result matters instead of relying exclusively on abstract experience points.

Mission progression uses an interconnected objective structure inspired by strategic planning systems. Objectives can have dependencies, while different activities contribute to wider mission outcomes.

An essential principle is that selecting an objective does not automatically complete the corresponding engineering work. Progress depends on the relevant action, system condition, or scientific evidence being satisfied.

This approach encourages scientific reasoning, prioritization, and active problem-solving.

7. Environmental Hazards, Operational Crises, and Mission Resilience

Mars presents serious challenges beyond the initial landing.

ARES-NEXUS explores several important operational risks, including dust storms, reduced solar power availability, thermal-management demands, radiation events, equipment malfunctions, communication disruptions, and shortages affecting critical systems.

The simulation incorporates changing environmental conditions and their effects on connected infrastructure.

Players must evaluate warnings, identify the underlying problem, and choose appropriate corrective actions.

Emergency responses may involve repairing equipment, adjusting power priorities, protecting the crew, or activating operational safety procedures.

The project also explores Safe Mode operations, radiation shelter procedures, and multi-sol resilience assessments.

Not every problem has the same severity. Minor issues may reduce efficiency, while neglected critical failures can jeopardize the mission.

Our approach emphasizes understandable cause and effect. A successful response should result from a meaningful engineering decision rather than a random outcome.

The educational purpose is to demonstrate that mission reliability depends on redundancy, careful planning, emergency readiness, and the ability to recover from unexpected conditions.

8. Technical Implementation and Development

ARES-NEXUS was developed as a web-based interactive application using HTML5 Canvas, JavaScript, and CSS.

The central visual system uses a 2.5D isometric presentation rather than a fully three-dimensional game engine.

This approach supports spatial exploration, visually understandable engineering systems, interactive environments, and efficient browser-based delivery.

The technical architecture incorporates shared mission state, event-driven interactions, simulation updates, navigation systems, versioned save data, and automated validation.

A central development priority has been ensuring that changes made in one part of the mission have consequences in subsequent stages.

For example, spacecraft configuration affects mission readiness, mission cargo affects surface supplies, and available infrastructure affects the outpost's ability to respond to changing conditions.

The development process also employs deterministic simulation behavior where appropriate, automated tests, version control, and iterative debugging.

The game is designed to operate through a standard web browser without requiring players to install a conventional desktop game engine.

Artificial intelligence tools, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and ChatGPT, assisted with software implementation, debugging, technical analysis, research, and documentation. The student team directed the project concept, engineering priorities, design requirements, and development decisions. The experience is based on programmed simulation systems rather than a runtime generative AI model.

9. Originality and Creative Approach

The main innovation of ARES-NEXUS lies in combining several traditionally separate educational and gameplay experiences into a continuous, interconnected mission.

Spacecraft design, launch operations, interplanetary travel, planetary landing, astronaut coordination, resource production, scientific discovery, and emergency management are not independent demonstrations. They are intended to form a shared engineering system.

The player's decisions create consequences that remain relevant throughout the expedition.

A mission with additional scientific equipment may deliver greater research capability but require more payload capacity, electrical power, and operational support.

A stronger energy system may improve reliability but introduce additional mass or resource constraints during mission preparation.

Likewise, prioritizing infrastructure development may reduce immediate scientific activity while improving long-term operational resilience.

The 2.5D isometric format makes these interactions visually accessible while preserving the atmosphere of an interactive space exploration game.

Our design prioritizes meaningful decisions, readable telemetry, environmental storytelling, engineering feedback, and gameplay that teaches through experimentation.

10. Educational Benefits and Intended Impact

ARES-NEXUS is intended for students, space enthusiasts, educators, and individuals interested in aerospace engineering, planetary science, and future human exploration.

Its educational value comes from encouraging users to apply systems thinking to a multidisciplinary engineering challenge.

The experience introduces important ideas from orbital mechanics, spacecraft design, energy systems, environmental science, life-support engineering, logistics, and scientific mission planning.

By connecting abstract technical concepts to visible consequences, the project aims to make space science more understandable and engaging.

Players are encouraged to ask not only whether a mission succeeds, but why particular engineering decisions produce successful or unsuccessful outcomes.

The project also emphasizes that sustained human exploration requires collaboration between multiple engineering disciplines rather than excellence in any single subsystem.

11. Scientific Transparency and Future Development

ARES-NEXUS is an educational simulation, not a NASA-certified spacecraft design or mission-planning system.

Its engineering calculations and environmental models use simplified assumptions suitable for interactive learning. Scientific references and gameplay approximations are distinguished to avoid implying that fictional scenarios represent exact NASA mission predictions.

The competition prototype demonstrates an integrated Earth-to-Mars mission experience with developing surface operations, scientific objectives, resource management, and resilience mechanics.

Additional development focuses on strengthening simulation consistency, mission completion validation, persistence reliability, visual refinement, and the final mission evaluation experience.

Our longer-term vision is to expand ARES-NEXUS into a richer educational platform in which users can experiment with different engineering strategies, compare mission outcomes, and progressively establish more resilient Martian research infrastructure.

Through PROJECT ARES-NEXUS, Lagrange Works aims to transform the challenges of human Mars exploration into an interactive learning experience where every engineering decision matters.
